sections.content: When I started this master, I realized [hl:t_r]I had a strong tendency to gravitate toward technical solutions in design projects. Technology was often the first lens through which I looked at a problem.[/hl] During the master I became familiar with the concept of techno-solutionism and its criticisms. I agreed with the criticisms, but agreeing doesn't actually tell me what to do instead, and that left me with a practical question: if technology is not always the answer, how do you still use it meaningfully in places where it can genuinely bring value? Two answers emerged for me during the master. [hl:u_s]The first is involving people throughout the entire process, not only during evaluation, but during ideation and problem/context framing too.[/hl] The second is connecting technology back to the body, designing interactions that involve physical engagement rather than treating technology as something that exists purely on a screen. My FMP became a direct combination of both. At the same time [hl:b_e]the FMP reinforced something else I value: realism. I am less interested in speculative future technologies than in improving systems that already exist and are available to people today.[/hl] For the FMP, the literature exposed a pattern/gap: successful embodied learning systems tend to rely on hardware most people do not have (VR-headsets, Kinect, dedicated motion-tracking-environments). If embodied learning was to become accessible for at-home learners, it meant working with devices already on someone's desk. With the FMP I wanted to address my approach to design processes. In earlier projects I often entered the process with a concept secretly already forming in the back of my mind. The research process then becomes a justification rather than a discovery. But for the FMP I wanted to do it the 'right' way, really be led by a method, rather than working toward an idea I was quietly carrying with me. I wanted to be open-minded the whole way through, by involving people at every step, just to see what that would bring. This went well, but it also created more stress. Without a 'secret' personal concept guiding the process, it became less clear where I was heading and what the end goal was. At the same time, it opened up far more directions and ideas than I would have discovered on my own.But it also made it difficult to recognize when to be a source of input yourself. As a designer, where do you draw the line between adding your own insights and unintentionally steering the process? Involving people closely also turned out to be subtler than just asking them. Early on, in a co-design session, participants told me they wanted something physical to hold while learning, something to feel connected to what was happening on screen, so I added it. When I ran the study, to my surprise, almost no one used it. What grounded people instead was seeing their own hands mirrored on screen through the live tracking. They had asked for one thing and been helped by another. [hl:u_s]It taught me to treat what people ask for as a clue rather than an instruction to follow. [/hl][hl:c_a]Looking back, that was also an aesthetic decision, the thing I was really shaping was not how the interface looked, but the felt experience of seeing your own hands move on screen.[/hl] [hl:u_s]Through my FMP I learned that technical expertise becomes most valuable when it is grounded in human needs rather than leading the process by default.[/hl]
